utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you have some preliminary matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Two very brief matters. Your Honour, I believe it was on Monday that you made a reference to the possibility of requiring the Prosecution to have a witness for Friday. We have identified the possibility or have been discussing the possibility with Dr. Fagel. He's a person who the Chamber has already granted us permission to call, and he lives in the Netherlands; but I would have to know before the close of business today. He's trying to rearrange his schedule. If the Chamber could advise us, I would do my best to make arrangements for Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask Mr. Alarid. We'll assess it at the end of the day in discussion with Mr. Alarid in relation to his witness list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could go into private session for the next matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit, and you may begin, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Hough.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Adjust your collar there. You're on TV. Excellent. Thank you. Please state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: My full name is Dr. David George Hough, and that's spelled Hough, H-o-u-g-h.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what is your -- where do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: I reside in Topeka, Kansas, the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And are you married?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes. I have two daughters. Their ages are 16 and 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And currently, how are you employed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: I'm currently employed in private practice as a clinical psychologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just along the lines of, you know, finding your way here to The Hague and the War Crimes Tribunal, let's kind of go through a little bit of your background. Have you ever served in the military?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I served in the United States Army from 1970 until 1973. During my time in the military, I was in the Army Special Forces, otherwise known as the Green Berets. I went through all the rigorous training that was required of that programme, and I was deployed to army special forces units in Thailand in 1972, and there I worked with radio operations as well as special operations with Thai special forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And were you discharged from the military?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes. I was honorably discharged as a sergeant of the rank E-5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what did you do after you left the military?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: After I left the military, I came home and matriculated to the University of Michigan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And matriculated, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: I mean I went to school. I went to college.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I say that because what made you decide to go? Were you living in Michigan? Was that your choice?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes, that's where I was raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so briefly give us your post-secondary education.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: I first graduated for the University of Michigan in 1978 with a bachelor's degree in general studies, and then I completed a Ph.D. in clinical psychology of the California School of Professional Psychology in Berkeley, California. That was awarded, I believe, as January of 1988, after which I was accept into a prestigious post-doctoral fellowship at the Menninger Clinic in Topeka, Kansas, in the United States. That was a two-year post-doctoral fellowship in clinical psychologist. After that, I was working at Topeka State Hospital as the director of the pre-doctoral internship training programme, and I also completed the Topeka Institute for Psychoanalysis Programme. I graduated from that programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Tell us a bit more about the Menninger fellowship.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: It's a highly competitive fellowship. A lot of people applied at that time. It involved very -- submitting a lot of work samples, going for personal interviews, which included not only regular interviews about background and so on but also clinical stress interviews basically to weed out people with some kind of character problems or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what about the Topeka Institute for Psychoanalysis?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: That's also a very selective programme. Usually one applies by invitation. I was invited to apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how long did you stay with this institute?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: About eight years. It's a very rigorous programme but also -- it requires a lot of time to get through it. There's four years of coursework in addition to ongoing -- a lot of supervision on the clinical cases, psychoanalytic cases, and you have to carry two psychoanalytic cases to full termination, and that can range from three to eight years anyway; and you also have to have two cases that have every promise of being brought to successful termination by the time you're done; so it's a very rigorous screening process. After the first year, there's a screening interview to assess your knowledge about psychoanalytic theory and technique and your readiness to progress forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you're board-certified in clinical psychology; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Tell us about what board certification is and why is that significant in relation to the norm.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, I'm board-certified by the American Board of Professional Psychologist in the United States, and that is the only board that is recognised by the American Psychological Association. There are other boards that are available, but this is the only one recognised by the APA. Board certification does require not only submission of a variety of work samples to include psychological assessment and work samples for psychotherapy, individual psychotherapy, but also a rigorous interview by a panel, which covers a variety of topics from clinical work to assessment to clinical ethics, research, anything they want to ask. It's a very -- it's a very demanding process, but once having obtained that process, it does confer for the public a level of competence that may not otherwise be necessarily assumed or by having the Ph.D. alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I think that you may have mentioned this, but is there any exam work that requires -- is required to get into board certification?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes. There are a number of work samples that have to be provided, not only in terms of one's psychotherapy process but also a psychological assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what about continuing education?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, that's an ongoing requirement that's required of all psychologists who are licensed in the United States depending on state. I'm licensed in the State of Kansas as well as Missouri. So both states have minimum continuing education requirements which have to be met for both states. One of the requirements, of course, is that you take an ethics course, but aside from that the requirements can be met in a variety of ways, and I've always kept current with my continuing education requirements. I'm currently scheduled to take a four-day course in April when I return in Wichita, Kansas, in forensic psychology.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm going to take slight pauses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid. I apologise. I should have said at the outset that in the absence of Judge Van Den Wyngaert, Judge David and I sit pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you'll hear us take a slight pause so that the interpreters, we don't overlap too much, and are they lose some of the interpretation for the benefit of the Serbian -- non-English speakers that are watching. So along the next courses, have you taken any forensic psychology?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, what is forensic psychology?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, forensic psychology in a nutshell is psychology as applied to clinical work that has reference to legal implications that will in some way be involved with the court system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So is this essentially your appearance here today under this umbrella of forensic psychology?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes, I would say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And have you made -- have you been a presenter on clinical or forensic topics?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you give the Court a relevant litany?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes. Let me get my glasses, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please switch off his microphone when not using it, and would you kindly observe the pauses between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Just looking at my own curriculum vitae beginning on page 7 at the top, and I would be going in reverse order, basically, panel presentation on the political brain, the emotional role of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just one moment. With the Court's assistance [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Alarid, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I've just been reminded to turn on my microphone. Could we have 1D22-0719, which should be their CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And although you have a paper copy there, Dr. Hough, it'll also be presented on the screen, and if you'd like us to go to any particular page reference, looking at the screen you can guide us.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Okay. Okay, you have the document, and if we turn to page 7 of that curriculum vitae under the heading at the bottom of the page would be entitled presentations, which would be the most recent presentation that I was involved with on a panel discussion. The title of the presentation was the political brain: The role of emotion in deciding the fate of the nation. The next one with forensic implications would have been the one following that on May 7th of 2008, the traumatised society, Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And why -- tell us about that one a little bit.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, the focus of that presentation was basically regarding -- to address the question of how does a society in a post-conflict environment begin to reconstitute itself? How does it begin to address trauma on a mass scale? And that was based partly upon my fact-finding trip with a colleague to Bosnia in 2005, I believe it was, or 6, excuse me, to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And where did you go in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Again, would the counsel please switch off his microphone when not using it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After arriving in Dubrovnik, we made our way directly to Tuzla. That was where most of our time was spent. We got to Srebrenica, which was very difficult, and then Sarajevo and left from there, so it was a very -- about a 10-day trip, but it was enough to gather some basic information. The next presentation following that, the case of an internet sex offender, 11/11/07. The one following that, March 28th of 2007, sexual predators on the internet; April 18th of 2006, trauma in post-war Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what was the topic of that [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was partly in relationship to the topic I just described regarding traumatised society. The one after that, evaluating PTSD, that's post-traumatic stress disorder in the international context.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And why would that be relevant to, let's say, this situation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: First of all, the situation that I was actually discussing and talking about was some work I'd done in Kosovo with internationals who had been ambushed, but it would be relevant to any of this discussion because very often people of other cultures are asked to make themselves available in a war-torn culture to provide treatment as best they can under often extremely harrowing circumstances. So the effort is to try to evaluate this phenomena under often very difficult situation and to provide whatever measure of treatment or prophylaxis can be administered at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, of what relevance is cultural sensitivity to exploring a forensic path with, let's say, a foreign national of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, it's very relevant. Major culture groups in the world obviously have their own patterns of language, social relationships, kinship patterns, concepts of being involved in treatment, accepting help. The differences between groups can often be quite divergent, so it's important as best one can to try and understand as much as possible about the culture into which you will be immersed and to be sensitive to the degree to which cultural miscues can occur, misunderstandings, and to try to be able to correct those as much as possible. We have that difficulty even in my own culture, which is actually a very multicultural society, people from different socio-economic strata, people from different ethnic groups, and although we live in the same physical space, we live on culturally different worlds sometimes, so it's important to try to be sensitive to this. I could go on through the list, if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Please, just briefly --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this is one that I'm not aware of the Court's ruling, is was there a ruling as to the expertise of Dr. Hough? I know there's been several challenges to him, so I think it's relevant to go somewhat into his background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm advised that we gave a general ruling that a number of experts -- a number of witnesses qualified as experts, and in that list is Dr. Hough. Is it Dr. Hough or Hough?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's Hough, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I saw you attempting to rise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We do not dispute Dr. Hough's qualifications as a clinical psychologist and what he does. We are going to go into some areas where we believe that he has stepped outside of his area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Good. Well, you can put that to him in your cross-examination. So he has been accepted by the Chamber as an expert witness for the purposes for which he has been called, and I just would like to make that clear. In any event, the Chamber accepts him as an expert witness. I don't think you need to spend a lot of time on his qualifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour, and so what I'm going to deviate to is more relevant work in the areas of which he was brought here and then move on as quickly as possible to his actual findings and how he made those findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just from a prospect of most relevant, what other, you know, either from a cultural and/or topic-related aspect from the list as we have before us in the CV could we get any more relevant ones you'd like to talk about before we move on.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: I might touch briefly just on range of experience serving with both prosecution as well as defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We could go on that, but we were in formal presentations and topic presentations. Is there any other ones that you would like to touch on?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Thank you. That is where we could go next, is tell us a little bit about your pathway -- it's my understanding you're in private practice today. Tell the Court what the break-up of your practice is.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: My practice consists of approximately -- 40 percent of my work is clinical work in a relatively small private practice where I provide individual psychotherapy and psychoanalysis for adults and the some adolescents of all -- from basically age 17 on through geriatrics of a garden variety of presentations. About 20 percent of my practice would consist of clinical consultations. These would either be to companies or organisations, or agencies of some sort. These typically revolve around personnel issues, organisational issues, management issues. And then the final 40 percent of my work is involved with forensic consultation and the evaluations and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: More specifically with regard to forensic consultations and evaluations, that 40 percent, how could you break that down and to what degree are you working on criminal cases for one side or the other?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, first of all, I would divide that forensic work into a number of do maintenance. The first would just be independent psychological evaluations: Insurance companies, government agencies, and so on. And then criminal cases, which of that 40 percent would probably constitute about 75 percent of that. Aside from routine garden-variety competency evaluations, I also for -- private attorneys, local, state, federal, defenders and prosecution, a lot of that criminal work revolves around working with violent crime: Homicide, mass killings, violent sexual predators. I also do some civil cases, personal injury, plaintiff and defendant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you call mass killings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My definition, sir, would be one single killing episode to kill more than one person. I had a case, for example, where one individual on a drug deal gone bad, basically, killed six people at one setting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then I also do some witness credibility work for prosecution and defence, looking at transcripts, evidence of CDs, audio-tapes, interrogations, Miranda issues, or courtroom observations of witness testimony. That would be the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are the issues that you typically address in your criminal practice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In relation to an accused person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The first level, sir, would be basic competence. Are they able to move forward in trial? Do they have the requisite psychological resources to do that? Aside from that, there can be a whole host of issues that may be involved, one of which might be mens rea issues, state of mind at the time of the allegation; and the degree to which that mind may or may not have been influenced by duress, substances of some sort, toxic products, the degree of planning and preparation and so on. There can also be a variety of other issues that I'll be asked to look at. It can be quite broad. They might ask me to look at mitigation issues such as developmental history or to what degree did a certain kind of abuse in childhood, in what way did that manifest in the crime itself, so it can be quite broad. Once you get beyond competency, there's a lot to be looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, we're going to cover two topics that you've mentioned, one being an evaluation of Mr. Milan Lukic himself; and secondarily to that, you were also asked to look at three of the witnesses for the Prosecution and for such witness issues. Let's talk first about witness issues. Tell us how you got into that, and tell me what kind of cases have you worked on where witness credibility or issues surrounding the witness became an issue.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, in many instances in my work, witness credibility issues are often quite relevant in cases where the only source of evidence is relying upon eye-witness testimony, when there's no forensic evidence available. It's basically one person's word against another. This is often evident with children, for example, in sexual abuse crimes but in other instances, as well, so that's how I have become involved more in the evaluation of witness credibility and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And with regards to [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And with regards to the actual forensic evaluation of a criminal defendant, tell us about the range of issues in terms of a full formal evaluation.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, they can be quite wide. I've been asked to do something as simple as simply go and spend time with a defendant who's facing an imminent sentencing that will be quite severe, and sometimes they anticipate -- the attorneys anticipate that this individual will have a hard time with that, so I might spend some time providing some supportive services to them to help that. That would be on the light end of the continuum. Moving forward, obviously the usual -- excuse me, the usual competency issues would emerge, and competency can cover a wide range of topics: Competency to move forward to trial, competency to sign a Miranda waiver, even competency to be executed. There are a variety of competency issues that are relevant in that regard. Beyond that, I'm usually asked to provide a comprehensive psychological evaluation. Sometimes the question is simply quite broad. They just want to know, what is this person's emotional and cognitive status at the time? But other times they might want to know something more specific. They might want to know character organisation. They might want to know capacity for certain kinds of acts; does the character organisation lend itself potentially to engaging in such kind of behavior? That's kind of a broad answer, sir, but it really depends upon the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, focussing you a little bit on your cases, how many times have you been called upon to review criminal cases and also testified or given depositions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: The total number of times I provided testimony and deposition has been approximately 63 times. I've been asked to review criminal cases far more times than that. These would simply be the number of cases that have moved forward to the next stage of adjudication. Often, they will plea out before that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you take us through some relevant cases that involve a wide range of suspects and their attendant problems?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: I would begin, for example, with looking at death penalty cases that I've worked in the State of Kansas and the State of Missouri. Probably in one that I testified on, which is a very difficult case, was the case of State of Missouri versus David Zinc [phoen]. Mr Zinc --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Tell us a little bit about Mr. Zinc.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Mr. Zinc - the case has been adjudicated, so I am free to talk - had spent 20 years in prison for a violent rape committed at the age of 20. He had been finally released to the community, and four months later he was violating his parole by drinking heavily, and he engineered a small minor accident with a woman which would allow him to get out of the car and have access to her. In the process of trading insurance information with her, he abducted her. To make a long story short, he took her out into the woods and broke her neck with a choke-hold. This was a man who by every light would be considered a stone-cold killer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Tell us about sort of the -- if you use that common term, stone-cold killer, what would be the more technical term and ...

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: The more technical term would be he would be a pure psychopath. He had no remorse, no sense of guilt or conscience about the event. What he was upset about was the fact that he had been caught, which meant he would obviously go back to the prison and face the death penalty. His concern was for himself, not for the victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What evidence did you give?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well actually where I came in on the case, sir, was actually on the appeal. I had evaluated Mr. Zinc right from the very beginning. I was initially called in because he was initially what's called a volunteer. In death penalty parlance in the United States, a volunteer is someone who has impulsively decide they had want to waiver all representation. They simply want to be executed. They want to get it over with now. The attorneys were very concerned about competency issues at that point, thinking this client is obviously perhaps demonstrating some kind of psychiatric disturbance in this volunteer mode, so I was initially called in to assess him for suicidal ideation and his volunteer status. That quickly abated and it became apparent that this was manipulative. This was really a cry for help and a cry for more privileges in the gaol and so on. I then became involved at another point on the case of beginning to provide a comprehensive evaluation of Mr. Zinc so the attorneys would have a good sense of where he had been by developmental history and where he was currently in terms of diagnosis, his cognitive status, the way he regulates his emotions, the way he relations to people. And then the next stage of my work was to look at the actual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What did you find?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that stage, I found that he was an adult anti-social personality mixed with paranoia, paranoid features, and that although psychopathy itself is not a formal DSM for diagnosis. The DSM is the nomenclature that we use in the United States. We don't have a formal diagnosis for that, but it often fits under the anti-social personality rubric. He was clearly that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down for the purposes of interpretation and also pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next phase of the work was to try to look at the mens rea issues themselves. That is, to try to have him walk me through step by step the commission of the crime: What was his thinking process, what led him up to the night in question, every detail of what happened that night, and thereafter. I have to say, however, my experience in that case and in other cases has been one where you do not get to that kind of discussion quickly. That takes a lot of rapport to trust as much as possible, to build with the client so that he can get to the point where he is willing to divulge to you that kind of information. He's quite comfortable talking about his childhood and this and that, but when it gets to the crime itself, that's a whole different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was your finding in relation to mens rea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My finding with mens rea is that he knew exactly what he was doing. This was a calculated decision that he had made on his part. His reasoning was somewhat flawed in that he assumed that because the woman knew that he had been drinking, because he had told her that he had a parole officer and he told her the name of the parole officer, that she would go and tell the parole officer he had been drinking and, therefore, in violation of the probation and likely be sent back to the prison. His decision was that the only way out of that predicament for himself was that she had to be killed. Any effort to explore with him alternative course -- pathways that he might have taken, such as simply say good-night, apologise, something, something short of taking her life, he couldn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Have you ever dealt with -- though it's traditionally known as a serial killer?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: On how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, we don't need -- I think that's a very good example of the kind of work that he has done. For my part, I don't see that we need to get more examples. Why don't you take him to the issue at hand?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, the only reason I was going to look at two is because you're going to be given some information about Mr. Lukic that from a compare and contrast situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ask him about the serial killer. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did work on a case in the State of Kansas, the State of Kansas versus Mr. John Robinson. I was not called to testify on that case because the jurisdiction moved to Missouri. It was a multi-state case. But I did evaluate Mr. Robinson on a number of occasions along with a voluminous amount of records that were provided on that case. This was a man in summary who would meet women online, on the internet, create conversations with them, and the conversations revolved around deviant sexual practices, sadistic and masochistic practices, and there were some women who were quite receptive to this kind of conversation. He would then arrange for a meeting with these women offline. They would agree to meet in some motel or something someplace, and the procedure that he would use would be that they would engage in their activities together, and then he would finally have them get into a large drum or a barrel, and they thought -- the women thought that this was part of the sexual game. What he didn't tell them was that there was one more step to the game, was that once in the barrel, he would then hit them with a hammer and kill them and seal the barrel, and the barrels ultimately were used to help -- in part of the pylons that were being used to build a dock that he was building on a small lake, so that when he walked on the dock, he would be walking on top of the barrels. I have to say, my outcome with Mr. Robinson was quite different. He was also a psychopath of the first order. He was very manipulative, very difficult to relate to, and he provided me very little information of use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just to go to the other side of why you were called, in what circumstances have you testified in cases involving witness issues, perception, or credibility issues?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, there have been -- I'll give you -- for example, I will find that. Just a second here. Well, one example is -- it's a little bit -- slightly off base, which would be false witness testimony. We had a man who made a confession to a crime for which there was good evidence that he did not commit. But more often, I had been asked to look at the tapes of adults and children who've alleged sexual crimes of one sort or another. Very rarely do these cases finally reach the stage of court. Often, they are plea bargained out. I think I have one here that may have reached the point of -- oh, on January 4th of 2008, I was called to testify in the case of State of Kansas versus Kenneth Waddell [phoen], and this revolved around the ability of a child witness to provide court testimony. And in that case, as well, I had reviewed volumes of testimony that had previously been provided by the trial to investigators as well as interview tapes, and so on. And in that case my opinion was that there were no barriers for this child to be able to move forward and testify, and she did, and they were able to get a successful prosecution in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And with regards to that, is there a science of the psychology that incorporates issues regarding perception and memory?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes. Those are separate disciplines within the field of general psychology.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just generally speaking, what kind of sources do you use, or what kind of resources have you looked at in researching for this case and specifically with regards to witness and memory issues?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, let me say that the amount of resources that are generally available to the professional in the social sciences at this point is voluminous, and looking at those particular areas, as well, is encyclopedic in terms of the magnitude of information that is available. In this particular case, just to familiarise myself not only with the case, the context of the case, the geography, the socio-political dynamics, as well as a variety of issues that may or may not be relevant to the case, I attempted to review as much of the information as possible. I work in a busy practice, so my time is not unlimited; but I did as much as I could, and I've provided a break-down of the various area that I looked at and some of the representative articles that I looked at, which I think in many ways provide a crisp encapsulation of that area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please remember to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We were just reminded to slow down a little bit. Let's specifically go through memory first because we're going to deal with the witnesses first, and then we'll deal with Mr. Milan Lukic last. Tell us about the memory and the resources that you reviewed.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Again, the amount of literature available on various topics within memory is voluminous, so one has to simply try to be selective and try to find representative literature that best represents the current thinking regarding literature in the field at this moment. And on page 6 of my professional literature review, I can summarise these documents, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Tell us about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, please. Tell us about some of them in summary.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes. The first document was by -- the author's name is Robert Kraft [phoen], 1998. The title of the work is, "In viewing" -- excuse me, "Holocaust Memory: Persistent recall of extreme trauma," which is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down when you read titles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the book "Viewing Psychology as a Whole: The integrated science of William N. Dember." It's spelled D-e-m-b-e-r. That article in particular was a study of holocaust survivors from World War II and to see if there are any particular features about the way in which they recall the memories that may be alike or different from the kind of memory reproduction we understand at this point with victims of post-traumatic stress disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What kind of factors might be attendant to the situation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Can you clarify your question for me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What particular features were they looking for?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, this was primarily a qualitative study that was looking at self-report of interviewed subject. These were elderly citizens interviewed at Yale University, and to try to provide a content analysis of the content of what they reported in their memory but also the way in which they reported it and the way and the degree to which the memories that they reported were infused with strong emotion or the degree to which those memories may have been fragmented. That's relevant because the literature on memories from post-traumatic stress disorder also address a fair amount of the degree to which memories are also re-experienced in a very strong emotional way. Sometimes those memories can be experienced intrusively, wherein the patient report that they really don't really have a sense of control over this. It floods them, as it were, and that sometimes, but not in all cases, sometimes the memories occur in a sort of fragmented piecemeal way. That's not true for everybody, but in some extreme cases, that is the case. So to try to look at -- and to begin to try to understand in general the way in which memories for a great span of time at this point would still be recalled because these are people who were in Auschwitz in 1944 and 1943, how those memories are recalled now as opposed to post-traumatic stress disorder victims. The next study I looked at, the author was Karen Nelson, 1998, and she wrote an article: "A review of recovered memories of trauma transferring the present to the past," and this is in a book, Contemporary Psychology, a journal of reviews. The next document I looked at was by a number of authors: David Ruben [phoen]; Ariel Boals, B-o-a-l-s; Dorothy Bernstein [phoen], and this was in 2008 and this was: "Memory and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder: Properties of voluntary and involuntary traumatic and non-traumatic autobiographical memories in people with and without post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms," Journal of Experimental Psychology, volume 137, number 4, page 591 to 614. This particular article was, I think, quite relevant and important because there has been several ways to conceptualise the ways in which post-traumatic stress disorders are reported and experienced by subjects who are experiencing this phenomenon. And one school of thought is one that has been proffered basically by a researcher by the name of Marty Horowitz [phoen] at the University of California, San Francisco, who talks about often there's a fragmenting process in the memories when they are reported back. This finding -- this study also looked at the same phenomenon but found that that's not the case as often as people think. So what they're basically saying is that in the author's view, there is no real reason to create a separate theory of post-traumatic memory that cannot be accounted for by a general theory of memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What is the general -- a general theory of memory?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, the general theory of memory is that when memories would be recalled, that generally they would not necessarily by in fragmented form; whereas the trauma theory, the special theory would have argued that very often they are. That can have treatment implications as well in terms of helping clients with post-traumatic stress disorder address their traumatic memory and the try to integrate them into their consciousness. The next article is been a researcher named Daniel Schacter in 1999. The title of the article is: "The seven sins of memory: Insights from psychology and neuroscience," and this is offer in The American Psychologist, volume 54, number 3, pages 182 to 203. And I might say, by the way, that I rely on the particular journal The American Psychologist because it is probably one of the most authoritative journals that are made available on the North American continent for psychologists. If you have to subscribe to only a handful of journals that would keep you current and abreast of the new trends in the thinking, this would be one that you would want to have. What Dr. Schacter goes through in his article is basically a number of the ways in which outside influence can -- outside sources can influence the ways in which memory is recorded and recalled later on. There are a number of what are often referred to as attribution errors, so that people will misunderstand in memory what is being encoded. A classic example might be someone is being robbed with a handgun, but because they have only been able to fleetingly glimpse the perpetrator and the whole scene, they might encode what was this that man's hand as rather than being a gun but as a stick. And that may sound a little odd, but that's a misattribution. That's a misunderstanding. And he goes through a variety of ways in which perceptions can be slightly altered in this respect. I also reviewed Darrel Bruce, Dr. Bruce, 1991, "Mechanistic and Functions Explanations of Memory." That was in American Psychologist, volume 6, number 1, page 46 to 48. This is more of a kind of cut-and-dry analysis of some of the neuromechanisms that are involved in memory encoding and processing. It -- I mean, do you want me to go through --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Not necessarily. I'm more looking into the ones that best reference what was behind your evaluation of, let's say, the three witnesses that were present.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Probably Schacter, and then also -- I really also looked at some of the false eye-witness literature as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Tell us about that, then.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: And there are a number of studies in there. One would be by Saul Kassin, K-a-s-s-i-n; and Anne Tubb, T-u-b-b; Harmon Hosch, H-o-s-c-h; and Amina Mermon, M-e-r-m-o-n; this is in 2001, and it's on the general acceptance of eye-witness testimony research, American Psychologist, volume 56, number 5, pages 405 to 416. Now, what these authors have done is to sample a variety of clinical and forensic psychologist to determine for their own experience the degree to which theorys of eye-witness testimony research have been accepted in the courts where they practice. The finding from this report is that in most jurisdictions at that time, this kind of testimony was allowed in, so it was in -- the purpose of which was to establish the general acceptance of that line of testimony. I also -- I would also recommend Dr. Elizabeth Loftus, and she's a well-known researcher in memory and eye-witness research. This particular journal or document was 1993, "Psychologies in the Eye-Witness World." American Psychologist, volume 48, number 5, pages 550 to 552. And I guess the last one I would reference here would be one by Dr. Gary Wells, 1993. The title of his article is, "What do we know about eye-witness information" from The American Psychologist, volume 48, number 5, page 553 to 571. And then I did provide a brief summation of relevant literature, which I provided to counsel on June 9th of 2008, summarising literature on eye-witness memory and identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, speaking generally, what kind of problems arise in eye-witness memory and identification situations?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, there are a number of misconceptions that have to do with memory, which I'd be glad to enumerate. These are commonly held in the general public, but cognitive science has demonstrated these to be misconceptions and not factually accurate. The first misconception is that memory does not change once it's been stored. The model here would be that memory is encoded like a tape recorder, that once it's brought in, it's stored, it's intact, and it can be retrieved in the same form in which it was encoded, like an audio-tape. The second misconception is that post-event information - that's information that's provided to somebody after an event has been coded, encoded has no influence on memory once its been stored. The third misconception is that memory is impervious to suggestion. The fourth misconception is that memory failures are a problem with retrieval, with the way in which memories retrieve, but that the encoded memory itself remains intact. The last misconception I will allude to is that memory does not deteriorate or decay over time. Now, I refer to the reconstructive view of memory, which offers a different analysis of these misconceptions. In the reconstructive view of memory, the thesis is that memory is not like a tape recorder, that memory can be altered and changed over time. It does not remain in its pristine form. The second view of the reconstructive view is that post-event information can influence memory. That is, later on what the information one has been exposed to, the conversations we've had, exposure to media and so on can have an altering affect on that memory. The third proposition from the reconstructive view is that memory is suggestible. The fourth is that memory failures can be a product of problems anywhere in the memory process from the way it's been encoded to the way it's been retained and the way in which it's retrieved and recalled. The fifth proposition is that memory is subject to deterioration or decay over time. And finally, this view is generally accepted among the psychologists who study human memory and eye-witness testimony. The take-away lesson, I think, from this reconstructive view is that memory is malleable. It can be influenced. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And of the literature that you reviewed and in kind of following up on you're saying that the view of -- the reconstructive view, rather, is generally accepted in the psychological community, expand on that lightly, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, I would refer in particular to -- there's an article in my reference list by Goodman; Redlich, R-e-d-l-i-c-h; Kyn, K-y-n; Gagtti, G-a-g-t-t-i; Tydi, T-y-d-a; Schaff, S-c-h-a-f-f; and Hahn, H-a-h-n 1999, in the book, and the book is "The Handbook of Forensic Psychology," second edition, and the title of their chapter in that book is "Evaluating Eye-witness Testimony in Adults and Children," and so that's where I got that particular reference on that. But to speak a bit more to that, this is a generally accepted view among researchers who study memory and eye-witness regarding the malleability of memory and have adopted the reconstructive view. Now, what I'm offering is obviously a schematic representation. It's lacks the complexity of a full theory what you would get in a textbook would have, but there are certain take-away points; so that the final recall, the product of what has been delivered by a subject or witness will in fact be in amalgamation of what actually occurred, which will be the main source of the memories. But along with that recollection of what actually occurred, there will be other features involved as well. These will include internal processes such as what has been intuited by this person, what they inferred happened, information that they have attained from outside sources, post-event information --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would object at this point. I think the witness is just reciting what he's read in a textbook, and it went far beyond the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it's a ground for objection, but my own view is that we have heard enough. Let the witness state -- bring him to the evidence that he has come to give. We have heard enough of his background. Personally, I'm getting impatient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just to make the proffer to relevance, but I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is relevant, but we have had enough of that. Bring him to the evidence that he is to give that relates to this case. She's waiting to cross-examine, and a lot of what he has said will come out in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And with all due respect to that, I agree, but just because there are different thoughts on the issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not allowing any more of this background stuff and his practice. We have heard enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: All right. Specifically speaking, let's take us through the stereotypical memory involving encoding, retention, or retrieval as a witness to a crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Listen, you did not hear what I said. Why has this witness been brought here? Why has he been brought here? Is it not to speak to an issue relating to this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let him testify about it. Did you not examine him when you proofed him in relation to the specific matter? We have spent an hour and 15 minutes on the witness's qualifications as well as his practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am fully satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I'm not -- I didn't tender, this is all the science, Judge. This is the foundation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't know how you practice in your jurisdiction. For my part here, we have had enough of that. Move right now to the relevant portion of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now I -- for witnesses that are under protective measures, we're going to use a pseudonym designation for them, but for those who do not, we can use their actual names. Now, just for foundational purposes, is it true that I asked you to look at the issues surrounding Ms. Zehra Turjacanin, otherwise known as VG-114; VG-115; and VG-63?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Let's first focus on VG -- excuse me, Ms. Zehra Turjacanin. Tell us what you reviewed before you got to work in this evaluation.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, regarding this particular witness, on page 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And before I get too far afield, Your Honour, I would tender the CV of the doctor into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And we will call up 1D --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 1D202, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, of course, we can see from the records reviewed on the first page, just take us through, and what were the most relevant issues you reviewed -- or, excuse me, records you reviewed in events of evaluating Ms. Zehra Turjacanin's testimony and presence in the court and her prior statements.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, I would say -- I mean, they're all relevant, obviously, but I think probably the most relevant would be document number 15, the trial testimony itself. In addition, I would say that at the time I wrote this particular report, I had not yet had the opportunity to review the second episode of testimony on November 4th and 5th of 2008; so that would not be reflected in this report. I was given the opportunity to review --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to any conclusions or use of that second testimony. He hasn't revised his report, made amendments, we hadn't been informed that he reviewed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, he just did it, and he didn't generate a report, but I think it's, of course, relevant any new materials and I don't fine it particularly surprising that the follow-up testimony might be given considering that it occurred at such a late date and wasn't part of the original package tendered to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But she has not had an opportunity to review it, to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Because, Your Honour, there's nothing to review. It's the testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yeah, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Let me just ask you. Dr. Hough, did the review of the most recent testimony of Ms. Turjacanin change your opinion at all?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Please proceed. What did you look at, and what conclusions did you come to, and take us through your mental pathway to your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, the document that I reviewed are enumerated on page 1 and 2 of this report, and as I indicated, I think perhaps the most relevant in my view would probably be that which is referenced to the trial testimony itself, document number 15. There have been various interviews with investigators and journalists and security forces along the way, but in my view it all comes together at trial testimony. Let me, if I may, just offer a comment as I get into this material, which is that I realise my writing style can be a little bit terse, but I want to say as someone who is also a care provider and a human being that my intention was not to attack these witnesses. I have great empathy for them. I've been to Bosnia, and I've -- I have a first-hand sense of how much suffering has gone on there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Please proceed, you stated that the testimony was most relevant, but also secondary to that I'm assuming earlier statements and history were also relevant. What kind of things did you look for as you did your evaluation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, one of the things that you look at as with any content analysis is the degree to which the statements are consistent over time. Now, understandably, with this many years it would be unrealistic to expect perfect consistency from one time of reporting on and event to the next. But there should be enough consistency to state that the thread is still there. So I look for questions regarding consistency and the kind of details that are offered. The versions of events that have been offered across time do not seem to be -- they, in my opinion, seem to lack consistency at times. There at times appears to be some intermingling of what was heard from lived experience. There is also, as I had mentioned earlier, there's an inherent problem here with I think the recall for any of the witnesses because there's been so much time that's elapsed, and that's just a -- it's no one's fault, but it's simply an artifact of the situation here; that we're dealing with events that happened years ago, and that in itself renders memories -- there's a decay process that can set in there, as I think I'd mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Of what significance are Ms. Turjacanin's personal injuries, her obvious trauma from her burns regardless of the source?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, I think there's a number of -- and first, let me say the degree of her trauma does permeate her life, and I think that Judge Robinson, for example, has been very sensitive to that and very protective, and I appreciate that. This is a woman who's been very damaged. And I also think that -- and I'm not saying that she can't testify or that she's incapable of testifying. I think she should have her voice, and I'm glad she's had that. But I also think that given the magnitude of the trauma, we would not be surprised that the trauma would be manifest in the testimony itself, not only what it said and the way in which it's said, the need for several breaks and so on, and I perfectly understand. I work with trauma victims.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speaker kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I also know that with trauma victims that often it is very difficult emotionally to recall and report on trauma experiences. First of all, the recalling itself can feel like a retraumatisation. It's a stressful experience for that witness to have to go into those memories whatsoever. And the degree to which that stress is heightened by anxiety, to that degree, the recall process itself can be subject to some distortion. Events may be reported in slightly different order, time sequences and so on. There can be misidentifications, and that by no means means this person is fabricating. I do not believe that for a moment. But I do believe that there is a process and a style that is evident from a trauma victim that will be different from that which you would receive from someone who's not been traumatised. It will be -- the style of the trauma victim will be more emotionally driven. It will seem more incoherent to the listener. There is a lot of truth in what they say, but you cannot always be sure of every detail.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] And in examining her testimony, you came to the conclusion that he exhibited these traits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You did. What would your conclusion be as to how reliable, then, in a general way would be the testimony that she gave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that in fairness and justice, have you to give her reliability; but at the same time, you have to balance it, obviously, with -- compassion balanced with a realistic appraisal of what is and is not being delivered, that you cannot assume in the same way you might with somebody who has not been through such experiences that she's going to be able to tell you in a way that you would like to have it presented in clear -- in the way I'd like to have it presented, in clear, logical, factual, the details cohere and hang together. That's not likely to happen. It means you have to kind of listen with a third ear to what is in there. I will say, however, that there remains for me one area that I remain puzzled by, and I don't know how to resolve that contradiction, which is the question of the report to the police station regarding the nature of the burns or the way in which the burns had been received. We have the gas cylinder versus the fire, and I don't have -- I don't have an answer for that. All I know is that I'm left with a question mark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tell me this. You did not clinically examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you say that in the introductory paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. So I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How significant is that? Were you to have seen her and to have been able to carry out a clinical examination, might you have picked up anything that would have altered the conclusions that you have arrive at without the benefit of that clinical examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there is always benefit, sir, in having that opportunity to have a clinical examination. To be with the patient in the room is quite different than a records review. That opportunity was not available to me, but I -- and I'm not sure I'd have been the appropriate person to do it, but I think if that had been available and possible, it would have more than likely altered my perceptions; and I would have been able to, at least under those conditions, offer a clinical diagnosis and to ask questions that obviously are not available in reading the records themselves. It would have made a difference, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In your practice, have you done a substantial number of what you call these -- the records examination as against clinical examination for court testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have, but in most cases, the ideal, obviously, is to have benefit of both the records and the clinical examination. There have been cases where the opportunity to evaluate the witness, the person themselves is not available, in which case what I have left is the records. But the best examination combines both. Yes, I have testified on records alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which one have you done more of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The combination, the combination being the clinical examination in conjunction with the records. That's the way I prefer to operate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just to kind of tell you where I was going when I received this is, in my jurisdiction we have what's called a 706 expert where we can petition the Court to ask someone to actually evaluate the person; but under the then-atmosphere of the whole case, I thought it would have been inappropriate to suggest such a thing, but it did cross my mind to say, Okay, would the Court be benefitted by an independent, totally neutral but someone that would actually bring those questions to close, but I didn't know what the process would be in this arena, so just to let you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, of what significance is it, though, that as part of the one of the main people that she accused of assaulting her as well as Mr. Milan Lukic was a man by the name of Mitar Vasiljevic who at this point in time was two weeks or so in the hospital and could not have been part of this trauma at least as if it occurred on June 27th of 1992; for hypothetical as well as realistic purposes, can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. First of all, it's a long question, and I'm not really sure that I understand what the question is, but what significance is it? He's putting a fact to the psychologist about something he believes to be true and is asking this witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: It's a judicial finding, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Not in this court. Right, but it -- the point is, though, that he's asking the witness to comment on some fact that -- how it would impact on the witness, and I'm not really sure what he's getting at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question is unclear, but we are going to take the break, and maybe the break will bring some light to the question, Mr. Alarid. And we are going to take a half-hour break, so we are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, I trust you have benefitted from the break and that you are now in a better position to formulate the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'll try and be concise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We can do this by hypothetical or assumption, but, Doctor, in this particular case Ms. Turjacanin also accused and continued to maintain the accusation against the co-defendant Mitar Vasiljevic who was found by his Trial Chamber to have broken his leg and been in a hospital for approximately two weeks --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This witness did not testify about the Bikavac fire -- excuse me, the Pionirska. This was another fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you saying? That the doctor --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Zehra did not testify about Pionirska fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Zehra accused Mitar Vasiljevic of being one of the perpetrators the night of June 27th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: He wasn't there. He wasn't charged with Bikavac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, he was. It was dismissed before a trial. He was originally charged.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: He wasn't in the hospital at that time. There was no finding. It was dismissed, Your Honours, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, it was dismissed -- let's put it this way. He's my expert. I'm allowed to put hypotheticals to him, and I can get the proof that she was accusing Mitar Vasiljevic as late as 2000 in the meeting with Mr. Groome of which the interview note was tendered at her earliest testimony, and also which I believe this doctor has reviewed that particular note. So I think it's relevant, and it's a fact that is in dispute in this case, I guess; but it's a fact that I think I can put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Put it on a hypothetical basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Hypothetically, Ms. Zehra Turjacanin accused another person of also participating in the events of June 27th. Hypothetically, this person could not have been therefore because he had broken his leg, and therefore, to a certainty he did not participate in June 27th; yet Ms. Turjacanin maintained that this person was also responsible for her injuries. Given that fact, does that impact one way or another your initial perspectives on this case, or did you include that idea in your evaluation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, to answer your complex hypothetical, the answer to the last question is no, I did not include that particular facet in my analysis. However, in that hypothetical a witness who claims a report on someone who was not involved, there's a number of possibilities to account for that; but obviously it's a false allegation which could be due to a number of reasons, but that in and of itself if you find that does begin to raise serious questions about that witness's capacity to provide reliable information about other facets of the event, for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in terms of a false witness, you said that could be because of a number of possible reasons. Can you give an overview of those possibilities?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: One possibility might be a simple mistake in identification. It's possible to see somebody who looks like somebody who was involved, and so you would have a case of mistaken identification or transferring perceptions from one person to another. You might have distortion due to psychological issues. You might have distortions due to visibility or other physical conditions that were evident at the time of the event. There's just lots of potential possibilities that would have to be ruled out.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are several meanings to the word in psychology. The one most commonly used in the term "transference" is involved in a patient-examiner relationship where the patient confers upon the treater and begins to behave in certain expectable ways as if that person were somebody else, a parent figure, for example. That's the common use of transference. But among victims themselves, there is also a phenomena of sometimes somewhere in the realm of mistaken identity of seeing someone who has certain characteristics or likenesses of somebody else and can begin to assume that that person that they're seeing is in fact -- is the person -- how do I put this exactly. They transfer properties of their perception about one person onto another person and assume that that second person is, in fact, the first one. It boils down to mistaken identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: As I understand in my modest knowledge of psychology, Freud was the one who had introduced originally the concept of transference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: And in his first study in his complete works in 1925, he explored other meanings of transference; for instance, transference in dreams. Are you familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I've taught courses on dreams, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Sir, the resource of the problem of transferring in daily relations, similarities among persons initially, unconsciously, even though this problem might come to the surface.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: So transference according to psychoanalytic theory is not a phenomenon related only to illnesses. It's a common problem which the psychiatrist tries to enact from the psychiatric interview.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Or the psychological interview.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me say first of all, I'm glad you're a reader of Freud, but I agree with you, transference is ubiquitous. It's involved in all human relationships. In a psychoanalytic process, for instance, transference can be worked with. It's a useful tool to help resolve conflicts for the patient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: But you know about transference - I interrupt one second - is also called -- there's a chapter in Freud called "Interminable Transference," which is to say one of the most difficult things for a psychiatrist is to end up the process in somewhat a right to a cure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: All of these discretions went to the problem of the relevance and importance of the personal interview in relation to the clinical psychology or the psychiatrist. You know that [indiscernible] a word called the psychiatric interview --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've read it, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: -- which is the leading work in American psychiatry diverging from European psychiatry on the importance of the psychiatric interview to evaluate patients or any kind of clinical diagnosis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: So in not seeing or evaluating personally during a clinical interview in which you could administer, of course, object the test or not but you could go through the various parameters of personality, the psychiatric interview or the psychological interview is crucial in determining in any event in addition to records the structure of the personality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree with you, sir, 100 percent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Is Allport also given sufficient elements through a theory of personality any remarks also, Gordon Allport, the founder of the American Clinic of Psychology the importance of an interview; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Second point, or third or fourth. The post-traumatic stress could be immediately released in the case of witnesses coming to trial. You have said so in one of your paragraphs in relation to VG-115. [Indiscernible] traumatisation will be played out on the witness's -- it will be predictable, you say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: And so that implies that during the witness time, there could be many emotional releases related to the former trauma.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: And this in the intensity of this release could really bring a steam confusion sometimes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: -- of sub-processes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's very correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: And even alteration of the language and words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's very correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I just want to explore only two important items, the relevance of the psychiatric interview, the psychological interview, and also the impact of post-traumatic stress in witnesses when they are called to testify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I add one point to your very lucid conversation, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which is that when the witness testifies, it's best when candidates -- it's important to try to manage that phenomena so that the witness is not overly traumatised by the process of providing their testimony. It's a delicate balance and they can become over-traumatised very easily without much pressure. Some people think that the opportunity to testify is cathartic and therapeutic, and I think that is true for some people, and for some people it simply becomes one more trauma.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I fully agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I would like to follow up and before it turns into a question, Your Honours, in focussing on the doctor's recommendation, one of the end points is that she be -- that psychoanalyst or that psycho evaluation be conducted because of the gaps in the ability to reflect on this witness without the benefit of that, whether or not it's this interviewer or someone more appropriately ethnically and, you know, appropriate for this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, as an interviewer, you know, it's for a hypothetical of this situation I think to expand on what Your Honour said is that the testimony, the reliving of it can be traumatic as well.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, can -- what affect with recurring trauma have on the witness? Recurring exposure to trauma relating to their experiences.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: If you're talking about witnesses who have been repeatedly exposed to trauma, multiple or compound trauma as sometimes called, it can become cumulative. One ads on top of another, on top of another; and you end up getting a condition that is sometimes referred to as complex post-traumatic stress disorder, very difficult to treat. These individuals suffer enormously, and in the absence of treatment, they will continue to suffer for the rest of their lives until some form of treatment and care is provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
