utterances.text: Now, as a clinician, have you ever had experience where a person who's experienced multiple traumas? Have you had those --

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Very often, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And as a clinician, has these persons, if you will, always exposed all the traumas to you at -- early in the process?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: It depends on the person. There is one kind of classification, if you will, where the trauma that they're living is so ubiquitous that they - as it were - leek trauma everywhere. The moment they walk in your office, they're practically reliving it and it's very obvious. It permeates the clinical atmosphere. There are others for whom repression has been more operative for them, where it takes longer to get to the trauma because they're very well defended against it psychologically. That's a different situation, but the cases where they've been exposed to multiple traumas, compound traumas, in those situations very often the trauma is very evident, almost immediately, certainly within the first 15 minutes, half-hour, and it's often profound in its manifestation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, to put it in perspective to the region, did you have experience either in your travels and/or in your review of the literature to see examples where war victims, victims of the entire theatre, if you will, in their entire time spent in this environment has -- could be called the multiple trauma scenario?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Again, the relevance of this to our three witnesses, it's a very nice story. It's very interesting, but it has nothing to do with why this witness is here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the relevance, Mr. Alarid?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think if you want to put it into perspective of all three witnesses, they all experienced a litany of things both personal and observed. They experienced their own -- often own assaults and pains. They also experienced watching others close to them in their kinship experience horrible things, and they also experienced a great amount of abuse at the hands of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm satisfied. It's relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just looking at the three witnesses collectively but of course we're on Ms. Turjacanin right now, is it possible that she's suffering from the effects of multiple traumas over the course of her war-time experiences?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, my answer is -- of course, I've not interviewed her, so I cannot base it on direct experience, but my inference from the testimony and from the records is that this is very likely; given the region, the nature of the conflict, and so on, I think it's highly probable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, what factor might social taboos or religious norms have on a typical patient in revealing things that might violate those social taboos?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: A prominent social taboo in the American culture and, really, I any in every culture is to admit that you've been abused in some way; sexual violation being perhaps the one most prominent. People are a bit more willing to admit verbal abuse or physical abuse, but there's so much shame and stigma associated with having been sexually violated that these victims are extremely reluctant to come forward and admit, and they will carry this shame with them sometimes to their grave.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, we diverged a bit in private session, but I would like to go back to Ms. Zehra Turjacanin. At -- what concerns short of further involvement of a psychiatric evaluation, what are the overall concerns regarding the testimony of Zehra Turjacanin?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, aside from the testimony, let me just say one thing. I'm concerned that she tells us that she really hasn't had treatment yet, and I'm concerned for her about that, but in terms of providing testimony, on several occasions, she's made that attempt but has found a need to take an emergency leave of an extended duration or a day when confronted with material that may be triggering traumatic memory for her or other kinds of traumatic responses. It may be that the whole enterprise of providing testimony and especially being confronted with trauma memories and trauma ideas and anything that in some way compels her to recollect and to think about these things is just simply too much to bear. So it's difficult to ask her questions about these kinds of experiences because you run the risk of over-traumatising her; and my inference is that she need to leave because the process was simply overbearing for her. It was too much to bear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, having -- having reviewed the [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Having reviewed the most recent transcripts, does that change your concerns? Does it add to your analysis in any way, before we move on?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Not really. I would say again, though, I haven't incorporated that second set of testimony into my report. She was a bit stronger second time around, I think, but she did also reach a point where she was up against or confronted with what was beginning to unfold in a tape that probably was simply emotionally overwhelming for her, and she had to stop. So again, it raises the question of the balancing between how far can you go into this material without causing harm to her. And yet if not questioned enough, then perhaps there's an imbalance on that side. So it's a delicate act. It's a delicate balance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I tendered it, but I understand the limitations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And moving on to 115. What factors about 115, VG-115, other than the reported abuse factored into your opinion?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: I think aside from the reported abuse and some of the difficulties in thinking that I observed from the transcript and thought organisation and conceptualisation and so on and intermingling of hearsay with what's been directly observed and some discrepancies between prior testimony in 2000 and current, I think the other thing that could not help escape my notice was that she had been found by that Court to not be a credible witness; and I just think that's a difficult position to overcome. So it left me with questions again about her capacity to provide the triers of fact with reliable and coherent information that's useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you find any significance to the fact that she - by some twist of fate - found herself at the two most -- as an eye-witness at the two most major accusations against my client, namely the Bikavac fire and the Pionirska fire?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, yes and no. The yes side would be it does seem a rather uncanny set of coincidences to be there. At the same time, I also understand that criminality and violence was so pervasive that perhaps one couldn't help but run into it sooner or later, but it was noted, the wrong-place-at-wrong-time scenario phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what significance was it that she seemed to be experiencing secondary traumas of witnessing horrific acts regardless of whether Mr. Lukic was alleged to have been involved?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure if I followed your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I believe she witnessed people being killed and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have a specific reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Please refer to your report. And on page 2, we're looking at it, she couldn't forget those screams, and it appeared that she was witnessing some horrible things. It appeared that she was witnessing horrible things on the bridge, from her statements. Of what significance is it that she may have witnessed summary executions, as well, in this theatre?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, post-traumatic stress disorder can be incurred not only by events that have happened to one personally but -- regarding life and safety and so on, but also events that have been witnessed, and the closer -- the more -- the closer you are to that event, the proximity, the more likely you are to be affected by it. So there can certainly be a PTSD phenomena that can be incurred by having witnessed a phenomena like this, let alone what has been done to her personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Of what significance is it that she also note that Mr. Vasiljevic is participating in the Bikavac fire on June 27th, that she has also memorialised this into her testimony and perception?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, if she wasn't there -- if she wasn't there, then the information she would be going on would be what has been told to her, hearsay, so there becomes a phenomena of incorporating hearsay into what has been directly observed and then reporting it onto authorities and third parties. It's possible to begin to incorporate some of that material into your own kind of experience and begin to believe it yourself. I don't know that that's the case necessarily, but that's certainly a risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is there anything else you'd like to discuss with regards to VG-15 [sic], and ultimately please give your final conclusions to the Court.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: I think that's probably it. I think we covered the main points. My conclusions, again, would be that the -- in my professional opinion, that the testimony that I've gleaned from the records raises questions in my mind about her capacity to offer triers of fact reliable and coherent information that will be useful, and I again note the finding from the 2000 court, and I'm not aware of anything in the intervening treatments or circumstances or anything that would have perhaps remedied that problem. That's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And for the record, we would tender the doctor's report with regards to his assessment of VG-115 at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll treat the report in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to make sure I didn't forget to tender it. And let's move on to VG- -- and I would correct myself on the record. It's VG-115, not VG-15 at page 67, line 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Please continue, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: But then ten years later, the name of Lukic is now interjected into the narrative now for the first time. So it would seem that if she knew him and recognised him, his identity, if she had recognised him the first time, she could have said so. Obviously there may have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Judge David has a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: I would like, Doctor, to get from you some idea of the role of repression, unconscious repression in post-traumatic stress, which is to say, as you so well know the role of repression in absconding even from rational thinking events that are highly damaging to remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's an excellent question. As you're probably well aware, the role of repression is actually at this point in time a very controversial one. Though it is well accepted in the psychoanalytic circles, I think in some ways that concept has been misused in some cases in the United States with sexual abuse cases, people who after many years have now reported that now they remember something that happened long ago and say the repression barriers have been lifted, and now I recall. So there's been problems with that. But in general, I agree with you that repression can be a powerful block against the actual recollection, and it would be possible, perhaps, to substitute a more anonymous aggressor soldier for the concept of who really did it, and repression could really do that for you. And then later down the line, years later, repression can under certain circumstances be lifted or repressive barriers can be overcome, so clarity of recollection can sometimes occur, but you do have to be careful about that because there are times when memories may come through repression, and they may be told with great sincerity and great emotional conviction and yet at the same time be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: -- the key to the method of reaction was also an initial Freudian contribution, which is to elicit by many ways in the memory part of the patient circumstances that will later discover the barriers to remember, and Freud called this a reaction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: So this, Freud said, is not an easy process because the repression in itself is unconscious and it's due to resistances of the complex that is there of curing the problem of memory. Is that -- could you elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely true. But let me also say a couple things, sir. One is just in general in the treatment of these highly traumatised individuals, we've found that every action is not enough. There has to be something that follows that, which we call working through, which means that the material is now beginning to come forward; but you have to do something with it. You have to find a way to help that person integrate that into their life. Also, there are cases when repression barriers give way too suddenly, maybe through an abreactive technique or some life circumstance. That, too can be very overwhelming to the person. But I do believe that there is unconscious repression, and I think that all of us carry a lot of things inside of us that we're no longer aware of, but under the right circumstances or the right kind of situation it will be back for us. But for some people, this is a very risky and scarey proposition for them. Have I addressed your concerns, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: The question I would like to, again, elicit from you is the role-play by repression, unconscious repression, and not remembering, amnesia, temporary amnesia or long-term amnesia of post-traumatic events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is -- again, it's become controversial, but that is very commonly observed clinically. It's not -- we have -- the general terminology we use with post-traumatic stress disorder is that we would call it delayed onset, meaning that for months or years later that this all comes flooding back. I've talked with many, say, World War II veterans who live perfectly unobstructed lives emotionally until, for example, they watch certain kinds of war movie, there's a number of them, and then it hit them, and it was overwhelming. It was as if it had all happened this morning, and it was very real and powerful. So there is that delayed phenomenon. There certainly is, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, was there any evidence from the statement from an inconsistency standpoint or just from your expertise that this was a case of repression versus a conscious decision not to disclose?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: And we're looking at 063, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object. I think this is asking the witness to get into the head of VG-63.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm asking him to do it on the basis of the materials he had available to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, he's asking her why something was said or wasn't said, and I don't think this witness can answer that question. In a particular circumstance, he can hypothesise and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'll try and reformulate to address Ms. Sartorio's concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, are you able to offer any scientific conclusion about repression in relation to this witness, particularly taking into account the fact that you have not examined her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, to answer your question, the fact that I have not examined her really does limit what I can say, and I would be -- to talk about a repression as it applies to her would -- it would be beyond the scope of what I could give --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please move on to another area, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, how significant is it, the fact that this witness gave a very specific physical description, i.e. tattoos, as a marker for Mr. Lukic well before any other disclosures and that if I were by hypothetical to tell you that Mr. Lukic had no such double-eagle tattoos present, how significant is that fact?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: To stay with your hypothetical, if there were no such physical markings like tattoos, and the witness claims to have observed this, then, again, this is a misperception of some sort. I would also note, though, it seems to me from a variety of the records, there is common reference to the double eagle tattoos, which would obviously be very readily observable for any man rolling up his sleeves or having a short-sleeved shirt; so it would certainly capture as a detail. But in the hypothetical, in the absence of those tattoos, it would clearly be a misperception and it perhaps theoretically could be guided by one that has been commonly discussed among others. So the common thread or the common perceptual detail that is agreed upon in the common discussion are the tattoos.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would a simple explanation be also misidentification, i.e., thinking someone with tattoos is someone else?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: First of all, it's leading; and secondly, I don't believe that he's laid any foundation to ask that question, just whether -- he can't explain why she said he had tattoos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Alarid. Ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, how do we address the fact that -- within the statements that this -- if I can't bring it up and ask the doctor to postulate on it? I mean, I think by proffer in the statements is this reference of a physical characteristic that is objective, let's say; and yet by proffer, we can say to a certainty that Mr. Lukic has never had such tattoos, and so I think it's a very relevant fact that was within this doctor's ability to comment on; and I agree that it's hard for me to get there without laying a specific point of reference which appears to be leading, but I would say it's not. I would like -- I think -- I'd like the doctor to address it, and I would like the Court's indulgence to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem I have is that this is closing argument, and he cannot ask this witness to comment on what another witness -- why another witness may have said something or not said something, whether it was mistaken, whether it was intentional. This witness just cannot comment on that unless he talks to the witness and asks her. So I think it's way beyond any type of hypothetical, and it is for argument, that -- counsel is free to argue whatever they want to argue in their closing briefs about this issue of the tattoo, but this witness is not competent to say what was in her head, why the statements -- what she said about the tattoo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree. I agree. You have to move on and ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can we go to page -- could we bring up [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: 1D22-0788. And could we go to the third page in the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, what we've put on the screen, Doctor, is your reports in this particular case, and you've reviewed a number of materials, and I'd like to go down to the third paragraph. Excuse me. And at the bottom of that paragraph, it appears that you considered the physical attributes of these eagles.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Can you tell me what page you're on, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Page 3 --

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: -- third paragraph, last sentence. And so taking as certain that she made this reference point, what significance, if any, is this in the final determination of your report?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, again, it goes to misattribution, you know, the physical attributes, which would go to questions about capacity to accurately recall and report upon relevant events for triers of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Other than what's already memorialised in the report, do you have anything to add with regards to VG-63?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Only this, that my view is that reporting on physical attributes are very important because they do certainly assist with identification. If someone -- I think someone is less likely to make a report about a physical attribute if they're not certain, and I think the more certain one is about those physical attributes, the more likely they are able to report it. So my inference is that she may well have been quite certain about that perception, whether accurate or not, but the certainly would likely be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we would tender into evidence the reports by Dr. Hough regarding VG-63.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It will be treated in the same way as the other reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just before I forget, and we're going to move on to the evaluation of Mr. Lukic, please with the court's assistance bring up 1D22-0784, Appendix A. I believe it was to the CV or the report. I can't remember, but if we could bring it on, we could identify it and tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Please identify Appendix A as I've uploaded it under a separate number, and tell us what the significance is of this document and to your report.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Okay. This is Appendix A, which I had attached to the report of Witness VG-114. The title of the appendix is: Background of the Problem. But what I'm really talking about is background literature regarding eye-witness testimony in memory, and I included that as a supplement for the reader to have some theoretical and conceptual assistance with trying to grapple with these issues about memory and eye-witness issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And Your Honour, for Appendix A, I would tender it as Appendix A to 1D22-0779, which has already been referenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And next, we'd like to talk about your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going to take the break now, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid. I imagine you're coming to a close now. Last lap.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We only have one more topic to cover, and it is the -- although it's more expansive, and it involves the evaluation of Mr. Milan Lukic. And, Your Honour, I believe we can remove the Appendix A, and I believe I tendered the three witness statements, so could we bring up 1D22-0735, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Doctor, you had an opportunity to evaluate Mr. Milan Lukic. Tell me how that came about and what you did. Let's start from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, I was contacted by the Defence to provide an evaluation on Mr. Lukic, and I evaluated him at the Detention Unit, UN Detention Unit here at The Hague, and I saw him on six separate occasions for approximately three and a half to four hours per occasion for a total of 24 hours, and that evaluation was supplemented by psychological testing in review of the indictment and amended indictment documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the procedures -- we're going to touch on the actual testing later. What -- but let's just go through. What relevance are the behavioral observations, and what did you observe, and why are they relevant?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, I think they are relevant because the degree to which the interviewed subject is able to engage in a cooperative and productive working relationship, that adds to confidence in the validity of the report. Mr. Lukic related to me in a very polite manner, very cooperative, very forthcoming. He was, I thought, reflective and thoughtful in his answers. I didn't detect any sense of evasiveness and so on. He worked to the best of his ability on the psychological testing tasks, showed good frustration tolerance and task perseverance. I did explain fully the limitations of confidentiality. I explained fully that I'd be writing a report that would go to the Defence attorneys who would be sharing it with the officers of the court, that I may well be called upon to provide testimony in open court and the results of that evaluation. He understood that and conceded to that condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And briefly, let's go to page 2, the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Okay. In addition, I noted just under the heading of Behavioral Observations, that I did have the interpreter services of Mr. Ivetic, who is currently co-counsel on the Lukic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, briefly and for the Court's assistance, could we go to the next page of the document that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That's fine. It's there now. Just so we can follow along with you, Doctor. What are the ideal circumstances of this kind of interview giving the issues of language, interpretation, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, the ideal circumstances, of course, are to be able to evaluate the client in your own office outside of detention -- or correctional facility. Also, the best situation is where both the interviewer and the subject interviewed speak the same language and converse fluently. That's not possible in this case. I don't speak Mr. Lukic's language, so I did need an interpreter. I was aware that there is the risk of dual-role relationship, since Mr. Ivetic is also on the Defence team; but the Defence attorneys assured me that they had exhausted resources, all other alternatives to a competent translator, so I agreed to go ahead and work with Mr. Ivetic. And I would say that I think he took his role very seriously. He was extremely focussed. He asked for clarification on any term or word that was not clear. He stayed back when he wasn't needed. He did not interject himself into the process. I've used interpreters before, and it's been -- you have to watch that sort of thing, as well, and to the best of my ability -- to the best of my ability to judge, he did a professional job, and the transcripts -- or excuse me, the interviews were all audio-recorded as an extra measure of reliability and memorialisation of the process. So the aggregate of my report as I believe is based on my information at the time from the multiple sources of data, the interviews, primarily, the testing and the limited records that I had at the time were that this was a reliable and valid report of Mr. Lukic's current emotional and cognitive status. I would also say it's important to recognise that we are evaluating a man who's been accused of crimes that are now 17 years in the past, and there's -- we're seeing more of the current man than the man we might have met at that time. There's no good way to fully capture the man he was 17 years ago, whatever that man was like. We're seeing a man who is obviously by virtue of age alone, he's more mature. He's living in a very controlled environment, and I think there are likely to be some differences, but these are unavoidable. So the task of reconstruction is one that -- it's ongoing, and it's inexact, but it's what have you to try to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And assuming on cross-examination it will be implied that Mr. Ivetic could have, let's say, not translated properly or anything, did you factor that in?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: I considered it. Obviously, I wouldn't know, but again, my direct observation was that he took the task very seriously. He was very focussed, very -- and had repeatedly told me in confidence, you know, he want to do a good job and he wanted to make sure he got it right. It didn't leave me with any real lingering doubts about his willingness to try to produce the best work product possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, what data were you able to obtain from the initial interview, and why is the initial interview so important before moving into the actual testing?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, several things. First of all, this is a man I'd never met before, and this is a high-stakes case. The risk of losing rapport with a client could be one that could be irretrievable if lost, so I wanted to proceed slowly and carefully. I wanted to build a foundation of relationship with him so that he could tell me in his own words about his life. I do move through the life in a rather systematic way, beginning from early years moving forward, and there's a purpose to doing that, but at the same time one of the goals I ultimately have in mind is that at some point we do want to get to the information that is perhaps most relevant to the Court, which would be the crime scenes and the mens rea issue; but that takes time and that takes cultivation of the relationship. And the first task is just to get a good base-line assessment of the client's current diagnostic situation and the life history, and I think we were able to accomplish that. There are, of course, as there would be with any reports, there are some -- there are gaps. There are some discrepancies that have not been resolved. My hope had been to be able to come back and see Mr. Lukic for a second pass, at which time I would have had the chance to then begin to dilate more specifically on some of the relevant questions, but before doing that, again, rapport had to be established; and I did need to get a good solid developmental history before other questions could be asked. I think we were able to accomplish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what factors did you find relevant ultimately? What -- you know, in summary of fashion, we have the report, but it's quite exhaustive. Let's try and boil it down to the most relevant factors that you achieved in obtaining the background and history of Mr. Lukic, focussing on the first few pages of your report.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Okay. The most relevant factors, I believe, in terms of the quality of his upbringing, the quality of his relationships was that this is a man who enjoyed a rather fortunate upbringing. He'd come from a very loving family. He was not subjected to any of the usual kinds of environmental situations that have adverse affect on development. He was not abused in any way. He was treated with loving care. His bond with parents was solid. His capacity to relate to peers was very good. He made a good transition to school. He did okay enough in school. He wasn't an outstanding student, but he didn't show any particular academic problems, either. He did make note of several things, of course, which is just the background reference to -- you know, the family had a hard time during the Second World War, and when that war ended then they were subjected to life under the Communist regime. Several of his -- both of his grandfathers, one of whom was killed and the other was gaoled for a while. This created a -- it's a tension point, but not overly so. But again -- but again, you know, the childhood is on firm developmental footing. I didn't find any of the usual indicators that would be signalling the emergence of deviant development or severe psychopathology.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What kind of things might we expect if someone was moving towards that path in the psychological realm?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, you might look at -- even from the very beginning, you'd look at the quality of the bonding relationship with the parents. If that was a flawed relationship, you would expect problems to emerge out of that. That would be become manifest in social relationships outside the family. You would begin to see behavioral indicator --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speaker kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You would begin to see behavioral indicators such as fights, delinquency, criminality, getting into trouble, moving into possible drug and alcohol abuse, identification with deviant subcultures. None of this was there. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What factors might be the close-knit family, being the youngest sibling of others and also the rural environment that he grew up in?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, two things. One is that this was obviously a very protective factor for him; having a close-knit family, very loving, the youngest child who was protected and seen as somewhat of a pet. He was very well loved, and he learned how to love. And I think that notion of loving and being loved is so important because it does have direct impact on capacity for relationship at later points in life and the capacity to find a loving mate at some point in life. I was also looking for indicators along those lines that would begin to indicate the possibility of deviant relationships moving in the direction of psychopathy, for example. Often when you really look at the developmental trajectory of the true psychopath, you will find that the relationships from the very early life forward have been flawed in many ways. This is not the case with this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And we touched briefly on the academic history [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We spoke -- you spoke briefly or began to speak about the academic history. Of what significance is someone's academic background in your evaluation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: It's significant because often -- childhood disturbance in character will often begin to manifest once the child has matriculated to school. This will also often be evident either by virtue of learning problems, learning disabilities, or attentional problems of some sort, which manifest in poor grades and difficulty following and tracking in the classroom, or conflicts with peers and so on. In other words, if the child is beginning to show problems, they will begin to manifest in the academic environment. As best I can tell --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speaker kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. As best I can tell, from all report about his academic history, he was a relatively well-adjusted student. He describes himself as not being a bookworm. He was not an intellectual striver. But at the same time, learning came relatively easy, and he got along -- but he was more social, and he got along with his friends --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that -- let's go to page 6 of the report that's on the screen, the sixth numbered page at the top, and that would be social history. What kinds of social historical factors are important to a diagnostician?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, I would look at the quality of his relationships with his friends. I would want to know if he had a best friend. Was he capable of having that kind of close relationship? For example, he did tell me most of the kids that he played with were Muslim kids. He did have a best friend. He was able to become heterosexually relate to a girl in the neighborhood. He was able to blossom towards relationships outside the family. Dating and socialising always came easy for him. He always had his pick of the girls. He's comfortable in a social situation. As best I can tell, he didn't really have any kind of problem -- I mean, any kind of problems socially, and he was able to relate to people of various nationalities: Croatian, Muslims, Serbo-Croatian, Latin America, Latin American friends. He makes friends easily. He was gregarious.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And -- we all know about the conflict and the racial-religious tensions that were in there, but would that be something you would normally touch on in, let's say a psychoanalysis of a States-born person in middle America?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes, and I don't find any evidence that he felt any special strong tension one way or the other regarding the different cultures and groups. He felt quite comfortable with all of them, didn't harbour any particular prejudice or certain preconceived notions or over-valued ideas about other people who were different than himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And if you were on a hypothetical analogy interviewing someone back home where -- do you actually ask them about racist tendencies or bigotry in their lives?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes, I sometimes, do and that's especially true for minority evaluations in terms of their relationship vis-a-vis the dominant culture, but I think it'd be especially relevant in the particular climate -- or the particular context in which we're extrapolating to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, moving on to the bottom of the page and the next page on the report. What, if anything, did you find relevant in his medical history?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Not much, really. I mean, he's a relatively healthy male. He really hasn't suffered any serious illnesses or diseases. He hasn't suffered any kind of prominent neurological problems. He's never had a head injury. He --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And -- just moving on, and I think this might be included, sort of, in medical is psychiatric history and drug and alcohol history. Those are medical connotations.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes, they do. The psychiatric history is fully negative. He's never been involved in any form of treatment, nor never sought out care nor never had it recommended, never been under any kind of psychotropic medication. It just hasn't been an issue. With drugs and alcohol, he denies having used drugs. With alcohol, he -- when he had access, he drank very little, which is kind of unusual in a culture that values consumption. He would drink up to, as he has put it, a half a beer at a setting to be sociable but not necessarily because he enjoyed the alcohol himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. [Microphone not activated] Now, the next section starting the next page, top of the page but the heading being at the bottom of the seventh page is legal history. Now, clearly this is -- we're in this courtroom, so what significance is legal history, and how does that factor in as a possible issue in your evaluation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, legal history is important to note. Aside from the current charges, what he reports is that other than that, there really -- that his legal history has been negligible, and I would ask that because whenever I'm evaluating, especially for the possibility of anti-social behavior, it's important to begin to look at delinquent acts or encounters with the police or juvenile justice authorities prior to the age of 15. He tells me that the worst -- and I ask him about acts as a delinquent for which he had not been caught, and he reported that the worst thing they had done was some of the kids would pick some fruit from a neighbor's tree. I don't consider that especially serious. But other than that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what factor -- I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: That was really it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But what factors might be apparent if someone is sort of showing anti-social behavior or psychopathic tendencies if that's apparent?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, if that were beginning to emerge, then you would begin to see -- you'd begin to see encounters with law enforcement and criminal justice authority. You'd begin to see the repeated violation of the rights of others at that early age. You would begin to see other -- you would more than likely see failure at school or poor adjustment at school. You would likely see the emergence of using drugs or alcohol on a pretty steady basis, identification with deviant sub-cultures, valuing crime as a way of life. Again, that's not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, we move on to work history. Tell us what you discovered and why it might be relevant in evaluation.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, I always ask about the work history because I want to know about a person's capacity to engage in a productive and useful endeavor to earn their own living in life. And in a nutshell, he values work. He's been valued by employees, he tells me, as a valued employee. He hasn't had long periods of unemployment. He works hard. The work itself, though, has been relatively manual for the most part, construction, working in local restaurants, making pizza. These are relatively work-day jobs; but he functioned adequately on the job, never been fired from a job, never been disciplined on the job, never been threatened with being fired, and so on. He loved to work. That's the main finding on the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, just in terms of the next topic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And we can go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: -- military history, and one of the things that jumped out at me was that you put his -- basically his early compulsory service in the classification military history. Why not include the full war in this -- under this sub-setting of your report?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, I think what I captured here was the first stint of military. This was the compulsory military service in the Yugoslavian national army, a 12-month stint. He adapted well to the military. He functioned adequately. He was honorably discharged. He went through the usual military training. He learned about the weapons that everyone else would learn. No special training beyond learning how to run a fire -- rocket operator. But he wasn't subjected to any form of military disciplinary actions. He wasn't -- he adopted adequately in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. And your next sub-headings that you note are martial arts training and weapons interests. Why are these some things that would deserve your attention and why are they relevant, if anything?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: I look at these areas because they can be indicators of aggression and how aggression is managed. The martial arts are obviously a very useful way to sublimate aggressive energies, but there are people who sometimes will use the martial arts as a way to either compensate for low self esteem or to gather skills that can be used in a reckless or more anti-social manner. I didn't find any of that to be true with the martial arts. In fact, he really enjoys all sports. He's a sportsman. In terms of weapon interests, I've worked with a number of people who have been weapons collectors and seem to gravitate towards a world of guns and weapons and so on, and that's not really the case for him. He did have a license to have a pistol as well as a rifle at one point, but he's not a collector. He said after the war he'd sometimes go hunting for wild boars, so this is again sportsman level of involvement with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What relevance, next page, please, for the Court' assistance, finally, your last personal section is interest in movies and/or books. What relevance is this to your analysis?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: These are relevant because I think it's important to try to understand not only intellectual interests and outlets but capacity for higher aesthetic identifications. In what way can he -- again, books and movies are again good ways to sublimate mental energy and to bind and contain it, so while he's not an avid reader, he does read, relatively light stuff. He's not a deep intellectual, and there were a number of movies that he had mentioned. He mentioned the book "The Bridge Over the River Drina," which is very popular, and I've read it myself. He also mentioned the movie, "Pretty Village, Pretty Flames," which I did later take the opportunity to review myself so I would know what he was referencing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you get any insights from watching the movie as to the subject matter and applicability to Mr. Lukic's life?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, I did because first of all he informs that the movie has personal relevance for him not only because it has a way of depicting the way conditions were on the ground at the time among combatants but more specifically some of the men who were trapped in the scenario -- in the movie, men are trapped in a tunnel fighting for their lives and that he knew these men, that the movie was based on an actual military event. So it had personal relevance for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And then the most major section which I think [Microphone not activated] ... excuse me, my microphone's off. The next major section and probably most relevant is his relationship to the actual war. What did you garner, and why is this relevant to this evaluation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, several things. First is that in Mr. Lukic's narrative regarding his life, he seems to bifurcate the life into two sections. There was life before the war, which was relatively tranquil, relatively -- he wasn't necessarily burdened by a high degree of problems or worries. But then along came the war, and as he put it in the first sentence of that section 2, the war changed everything. So in his view, things did change for him and for the world thereafter. But his induction to the war came rather slowly. He had been living in Europe at the time. When he began to hear about the war, actually, he was in Switzerland, I believe, and began to get media reports on the television; and he and his friends from all parts of the former Yugoslavia would gather together to watch this, often in disbelief, and he and his friends were shocked by what they were seeing. But he also began to describe a process where he really didn't take sides at that point, and he gave money to refugee causes, regardless of whose particular group it involved. He just want to go wherever there was girls and dancing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How did he describe his induction into the war?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, albeit rather slowly, but when he finally made his way back to Visegrad, he wanted to check on his parents. He was worried about them because they were obviously in a combat zone, and when he arrived in Visegrad, he met some of his old comrades to include his school professor that he had revered, and the professor was, I believe, in charge of the police brigade at that point and began to tell him what was going on. He simply want to go visit his parents and see how they were doing, but in order to be able to get authorisation to travel in the combat zone, he had to wear a uniform, and that was really the beginning. And he soon found himself in a uniform carrying a weapon and following the orders of the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can we just for reference go to page 13, at the top of the document that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: This is just by reference I think where you were paraphrasing from your report.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes. He was trying to tell the chief or former teacher, as well, he'd found a girl. He want to marry her, wanted to take his parents back to Belgrade to get out of the war, and the chief began to explain to him that people were returning to the region from all over the world, United States and everywhere, and that there was a subtle pressure exerted upon him to arouse Serbian nationality. Mr. Lukic explains that he didn't really want to go along with this, but he thought the uniform was the passport to get to his parents, and when I ask him in the third paragraph down how he felt once he had the uniform on, he responded: "I didn't know any better. I thought it was a game." And I note this because he was slow seemingly to catch on, that there really was a war coming, and this climate was becoming very dangerous very quickly, and it didn't seem to quite register with him yet. And I'd later ask him, When did it become serious? And this was not really until the Uzice Corps was about to leave, and then he realised that this was real and this really was going to happen. But there is a passive kind of in-tow quality about his induction. It's really what some people would describe as role induction. He went along. He went along with the flow, with the mobilisation; and he was with the chief, and he found himself going with the chief, here and there, and next thing you know without police training or experience in this area, he's helping round up people and bring them for interrogation. So it really began from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just -- could we go to the next page, please, on the computer screen, and actually, page 15, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, at some point in time the Uzice Corps left Visegrad, and it changed for him a little bit. Tell us about the next disclosures and why that might be relevant to your report.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, he describes it as the Uzice Corps was preparing to leave and then ultimately did leave, that this created a power vacuum that was to be filled by local police, and panic ensued. In an environment like this as tensions mounted, groups would -- respective ethnic groups would begin to cluster unto themselves and experience the other group that they had prior to this conflict related to in harmony and civility as a potential enemy that would take -- that would bring harm to them if they in some cases did not bring harm to the enemy first. So it really became, in my view, a break-down of social authority and civil -- the civil institutions, the institutions that are normally designed to protect the citizenry, such as the police and to keep the wheels of society functioning all begin to break down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: There was a -- excuse me. There was a discussion about the White Eagles and their role at this early phase in the war. How did that come about, and tell us.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: I may have either asked him, or he may have mentioned it. I'm referring back to page 15, the bottom paragraph. He was describing that when the Uzice Corps left, that there was a group that was -- that stayed behind who -- and, again, I'm reporting what he's telling me, that there was a group that was left behind by the name of the White Eagles, and he informed me that the White Eagles consisted of approximately 50 to 80 individuals who had fought in major combat engagements throughout the region. They'd sort of move from conflict to conflict, and that their commander had been a former legionnaire. I'm assuming that was French legionnaire, but I'm not sure, and that no one could really approach them at the Vilina Vlas Hotel. And he informed me that his commander -- that the commander of the White Eagles received personal instructions from the chief of police, and I took probably one of the first opportunities, because it would take many opportunities, but I took one of my first to ask him about his alleged involvement with the White Eagles while he was in Visegrad. And he denied it, and he went on to exclaim that he never approached them nor did he drink with them. His own view of them, the White Eagles, were that they were, in his words, druggies, criminals, bad apples, that their leader had been, again, a former legionnaire and that the deputy of the White Eagles was a retired colonel from the Yugoslavian army. He went on to explain that he didn't go into the hotel where the White Eagles were located. No one really knew much about them. He just knew that they were there, and they'd stayed until if end of July. So again, his report to me is he's disavowing connection with that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in describing the command structure, I note that you have a Chief Savovic, Brano. Are you sure it's not Branimir Savovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: It may be. I may have miscopied it in my writings. I can't be certain about that. That's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how did his disclosure regarding the war wrap up?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Wrap up. Okay. I guess to make a long story short, he described that -- he became increasingly dissatisfied with the role that he was involved with in Visegrad. He became quite hurt and disillusioned when his commander and several of his friends were killed and that he finally got out of Visegrad area and went into action behind the lines with the military and then went on to tell me about those kinds of experiences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did he tell you about his other duties as a police officer before he transferred to the military?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Let me see. I don't really recall in detail about -- well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I guess to refer you to your report, page 17.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Okay, let me look.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Okay. He described that -- there were lists of extremists who were to be rounded up. In his report is that the extremists -- the rounding up of the extremists would have been left to the older professional police or military, not to people like him. This was to be done by the pros. He also described that in his role as a policeman, in conducting his duties, that when he would go to the residence, he would always introduce himself, give his name. That he did this because he was trying to follow what he believed to be the role of policemen, and that policemen all over the world when they come to the home, legitimate policemen will introduce themselves: I am Officer so-and-so. So he thought that's the way it's supposed to be done because he had no training as a policeman. And he described other scenes that he saw and so on, trucks leaving with cargo going north and so on. But his role of policeman as he describes it was relatively low-level, rather circumscribed, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. And as he transferred from the police to the military, describe that and his relationship with the SDS party, if any.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: First of all, he described that he was relieved to be away from the police and out of Visegrad, though the duty he was now embarking upon was far more dangerous behind the lines. It was still a relief to be away from where he had been. He saw a lot of combat, almost continuously for a while. He acknowledged that he took lives in combat. As best I can tell from his report, however, his description s of those incidents would have been within the customs and conventions of warfare. People kill each other in combat. But he denies, and I ask, specific acts that would have been indicators of atrocities or shooting unarmed, surrendering soldiers and so on, that these acts were within the confines of conventionally understood combat. What was the next part of your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, before he -- there was a point in time where he was I guess detained in Uzice prison in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yes. He was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I'm referring you to page 20 of your report.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Okay. He was arrested and detained and spent some time -- page 20. Can you show me what paragraph you are, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... right there, first paragraph or first full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sorry. Didn't turn on my microphone. First paragraph, middle of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah. He described that he'd been arrested and in his view set up by the authorities. Then he was taken to prison in Serbia. He spent eight days there and then was returned to Visegrad, and his view is that the purpose of this brief imprisonment was to send him a message; and he described how scared he had been by that message, and he referred back to this is the sort of thing that you would have expect to see in the Stalinist era, but it was happening now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That's fine. And just basically, what did he disclose to you about chain of command, the authority structure that he was obligated to?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: You know, I'd have to look at my notes, quite honestly. He offered many, many details about that, and I couldn't keep track of every single individual in the order and so on. What I noted to myself was that obviously in his perception there was a chain of command. It was very -- he had pretty extensive knowledge of that chain of command of these individuals and their roles and responsibilities and their behaviors. He was eager to be able to disclose what he knew about that chain of command, and I -- you know, one hypothesis I entertained was that just as it's easy to try to push responsibility down the chain of command, it's also easy to try to push it up the chain of command. So I wasn't sure if, is he simply trying to distance himself by blaming it on superiors? So there was a lot of the details I did not get about exactly who related to who.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And tell us about his -- as we're on page 21, his reflections on his war experiences and time behind enemy lines.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: The gist of this is that Mr. Lukic felt -- it was reported to me, that he had done his duty, but he had not enjoyed the war. And after he had taken his first life in combat, he realised, and sometimes one doesn't realise until you've done this, he realised that he really didn't want to take more life. But nevertheless, he was a very active combatant. He was at times fearless or even reckless, I would say. He became very active as a fighter and sometimes would say, in quotes, We hit them very hard. So he was a warrior, but again denies to me engaging in acts that might be considered atrocities or outside the scope of legitimate acts of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You qualified by saying denies to me. I'm sure you're going to get touched upon by that statement and what it means to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure what else to say about it other than this is what the man is telling me, but what he's telling me is a consistent narrative all along.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The next -- on page 24, the next section of your report is the effect of propaganda on his perceptions. Why would you give this its own separate heading?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: I want to ask about propaganda because I had read in my own background reading about the environment at the time that propaganda had played a very prominent role in the degree to which it influenced ethnic polarisation and mobilisation of tensions and hatred. Various groups would use their own propaganda media to fuel dissent and demonise the other groups; so I wanted to get a sense of to what degree had Mr. Lukic himself been not only subjected to propaganda but to what degree had he internalised it and had used it as an operating motivator for his own behaviors. And he did explain know that the propaganda, the information that was coming into the area at the time was dominated by the Serbs, and so he was getting whatever was on offer from that source. But he also had gone on to tell me that he didn't feel that he had been necessarily overly influenced by it. I mean, I think at one point he had said, you know, Only the rural peasants, really, would be influenced by this kind of stuff. So he was neither an ardent nationalist or culturalist or idealist before the war, and by -- again, I find no evidence that the propaganda had turned him into one. It may have had that effect for some people but not for him. He had lived too long in a multicultural society to believe in some of the more primitively tinged ideas that were being propagated. He did see a number of quite horrific images that were portrayed on the television, of all places of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And where I was going to go with that is simply that -- what -- what relevance is it that he says that only rural peasants, but he came from a modest rural background. Did you incorporate that into your analysis?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, I think one line of reasoning would be that he wanted me to know that he had risen up, that maybe that was his humble origin, but he had risen above that. I mean, this was a man who had gone to school, unlike some peasants. He traveled in Europe. He had seen the world, and he had made his way, and he had had productive work far away from the peasant origins; and he had interacted with people from all over the world of all walks, and he had met a girl who was from an upper-middle-class family that he was going to marry, so he really wasn't that peasant anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, the next section on page 26 that you touch on is an important one because it involves an incident that also resulted in an in absentia criminal conviction, if you will or an incident. Yes, so you touch on that, though, and why did you touch on that specifically? Was that by your prompting or the reporting of the witness?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, let me say this incident which I had labelled as the bus incident refers to the - if I'm pronouncing this correctly - the Severin village. I didn't ask about this. In fact, I didn't have records about it, so I didn't know about this. This is what was report to me by Mr. Lukic, and the reason I put it in is because in the course of the interview, this became something that he felt was very important for me to understand, to get a sense of not only allegations that he's confronted with but also his involvement in an incident. But in the course of an interview, especially building rapport with a client, sometimes you do have to let them have a little latitude; and this was important enough for him that he want to talk about it, so I was willing to allocate the time. Let's talk about this, then, if you want to tell me. He felt it was important for me to have that information if I'm going to understand him, and so I documented that discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Alarid, I should tell you that the estimated time for examination-in-chief is three hours, and at ten minutes after 7 you'll have exhausted that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must conclude the examination-in-chief by that time. Three hours is more than enough. You must learn to manage your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I was trying to, Your Honour, and just considering we had four topics to discuss, this is the most important considering it involves the accused, Your Honour, and if it does bleed over into tomorrow, I hope that you would be indulgent, but I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How did you incorporate the Severin incident into your analysis, if any?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: At this point, I don't know that I've fully incorporated it yet. I don't think my understanding of Mr. Lukic is as complete as I'd like to have it. I haven't had a chance to reconcile what he's told me about this event with other records and so on. What I could say at this point is that this is an effort to -- he wants to be understood, and he saw me as somebody who might be capable of understanding him. So whatever is involved with this incident has high value and high meaning to him, and he wanted to give this to me. I don't know what I will do with it yet, but he want to give that to me, and sometimes an interview, it's almost like a gift, when a client wants to give you this piece of information that you didn't know about and hadn't thought about inquiring into. But he wants me to know, I think, that his roles in this region of the world at the time were complex and multifaceted; that there were times when he tried to help people, and he feels that he paid a price for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Moving forward to page 29. It's the first -- where you first beginning your interview confrontations. Tell us about that, and why is that important in this type of situation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Well, it was important because I want to begin to take a first pass at beginning to confront him with some of the obviously glaring discrepancies that would be evident between what I'm reading from the records and what he's telling me in interview. And I point blank ask him about the magnitude of the -- oh, okay. I wanted to just see how he would begin to respond to confrontations, the difference between what he's told me and what the world is saying. And I -- this is an area that needs to be explored more, I think. So I think his first reaction was somewhat defensive, but, you know, describing that, They've accused me of having tattoos, being a drinker, having blue eyes and so on, misidentifications. And he again denied involvement with the White Eagles. When I confronted him about all these charges, I mean, basically that they're not true. So that's the first attempt at trying to ferret out what is and what is not the case with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: When you say first attempt, why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Because I think in a case like this, to really understand this, you need multiple attempts. When I mentioned earlier in testimony the Zinc case, for example, I interviewed that client on a number of occasions before we got to crime scene information. So it would be unrealistic, really, to expect at this point anything more than I think what we got first time around.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, and I'm sure you're going to be confronted with the issue of the accused has an interest in possibly misdirecting you as a potential expert witness or a clinician. How do you accommodate for that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: I think that's always a valid question. I mean, that's a first-line assumption. In many cases, that's true, but I think it's an open and empirical question as to how that is ultimate -- those issues are ultimately resolved. I myself would probably make some kind of assumption like that, too, but eventually the data will tell the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so let's get into the data. The next section starting at page 31 is the results of the psychological testing. Why don't you take us through what you're looking for, and this is where we can go step by step.

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Okay. I want to -- with the testing, and I use the testing to supplement the interview, I wanted to get some rough measurement, as it were, about his functioning outside of direct interview; and I brought a number of instruments which I'm comfortable with, I've been trained on, and in my training in the past, I've -- especially at the Menninger clinic, we had patients coming from all over the world, so we had to have a methodology to accommodate to them. And the rationale there are there really aren't many instruments outside of those that we know and use in North America that we know and understand, so we have to use what we have and acknowledge limitation and so on. Yes, obviously, with the first one, the Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence, of course, this is normed on a North American population, but it does provide a rough indicator of non-verbal intelligence; and I made a clinical decision to use that. I didn't use the verbal components because it would be confounded by language difficulties. The finding on this was that within a confidence interval of 95 percent, his intelligence would fall somewhere within a range of 79 and 90. But I also -- but his activities of daily living and his level of academic achievement, reported history would probably put him somewhere within the average range. I think it would be very unlikely to see this man had above-average intelligence. Also, the non-verbal test also can give rough indicators of organic problems if there are problems with managing some of the visual spacial motor tasks. That wasn't evident. I also was very -- realised I really need to look at personality issues, issues that could be somehow looked at that would have some validity across time, so I looked at -- okay. I deployed several instruments that would be helpful in that regard. I used the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV Axis II Personality Disorders. I went through that instrument with him. And I also made a particular effort to focus on anti-social personality as well as narcicisstic personality; and I didn't find a diagnosible diagnosis from there. Certainly not of these two particular personality disorders, each of which would have probably the most relevance to the accusations. The Incomplete Sentences Blank is also something that I routinely give. It can be administered rather frequently -- or excuse me, rather quickly, but it also can capture in a very expedient fashion certain attitudes and concerns that a client might have and here other than his comments about regretting having being part of the war there was nothing no other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Doctor, we only have another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you do anything in relation to leadership qualities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. The leadership -- well, several things. One is from the MCMI, that's the next test down, the findings I got from that are that while he's certainly a very compulsive man and strives to please and wants to put his best foot forward, that, again, he's more than a follower than a leader, but he wants to please authority. But aside from that, I think -- you also have to look at the life course itself, and that may be even the most accurate indicator, I think, and as best I can tell, throughout the life of this man, I find no indicators that he has assumed any -- any position of leadership, nor has he initiated any kind of project or instilled some sort of motivation in others. The level of his work has all been low-level work-a-day. In school and other places, he has described himself as the man in the middle, the undistinguished middle, the man in the middle, the undistinguished man is not the leader. He's the follower or he's the man that goes with the flow, but he's not the leader of the flow. My best construction of this man with all the data is that he's a follower and not a leader. Now, that's the best I can give you, sir, is that I don't see -- usually with a leader, they will begin to differentiate themselves even quite early in life or maybe with certain circumstances they will begin to surge forward and show that leadership capability. It's not there, nor has he been through any kind of training opportunity other than, perhaps, the military that would have afforded the opportunity to learn leadership skills, but even in the military, he was a low-level, enlisted man who made no particular effort to advance beyond what was expected of him. He didn't take on extra initiative or apply for office or candidate school or do anything that a leadership man, even of humble origins, would want to do to rise and become a leader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Alarid, you had planned to ask questions about leadership, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because you only have another three or four minutes. I have to deal with some administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just with regards to the literature that you revolved yourself around in terms of this, you've used the term "ordinary man."

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What would we talk about with regards to the ordinary man?

utterances.speaker: DAVID GEORGE HOUGH
utterances.text: Sir, let me just try in a very quick, condensed way summarise the relevant literature regarding this kind of phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How is it relevant in you're saying the accused is an ordinary man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By and large, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you must get that evidence. The thing is not in a vacuum. We're not here to study the personality of Mr. Lukic, only what is relevant. Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The quest to understand who are the perpetrators of genocide really followed World War II when people were looking for the so-called Nazi personality. The assumption at the time was that these people must be either extreme psychopaths or deeply psychologically disturbed, or how else would you explain their kind of behavior? The problem that emerged from that is upon examination of most of these men, Nuremberg and some of the lesser trials. It became evidence that rather than their being monsters, they were by and large ordinary men who did not deviate outside a relatively narrow range of ordinary psychopathology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Maybe I interrupt you for a minute. Have you discussed in your report, or are there some reference in relation to what a normal course, the authoritarian personality?
